title: The Best Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers, Tested With 8,800 Leaves
gist: WIRED's hands-on test of battery leaf blowers picks Ego's 880 CFM as best overall, Skil as budget pick, Husqvarna 350iB for power plus run time and Ryobi 40V as best system, concluding run time is the core trade-off and that battery-platform ecosystems matter more than small performance gaps. Noise bans and battery advances are eroding gas blowers' appeal.

themes.theme: Battery displacing gas in outdoor power equipment

insights.claim: Rising noise bans, hard-to-start gas engines and battery advances are cutting into gas leaf blowers' appeal, though gas backpack blowers still win on run time for very large properties.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Regulatory and tech tailwinds favor cordless OPE makers over gas-engine incumbents.
insights.quote: Gas blowers have long been the standard, but rising noise bans, finicky engines that are hard to start, and battery advances are cutting into their appeal.
insights.locator: Leaves are a problem of addition

insights.claim: Tested battery blowers measured 78.6 to 95.2 decibels at 30 inches, versus 100-110 decibels for a typical handheld gas blower, with a 10-decibel increase perceived as roughly twice as loud.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Large noise advantage supports battery adoption as municipalities restrict gas equipment.

insights.claim: Run time remains the primary trade-off for battery blowers: Ego's top performer lasted just over 11 minutes on high and Ryobi's about 12 minutes, versus about 33 minutes for Skil and Husqvarna.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Battery energy density is still the gating factor, driving multi-battery kit sales.
insights.locator: Today’s models deliver serious clearing power

insights.claim: The reviewer argues buyers should prioritize the breadth of tools sharing a battery platform over small performance differences, and existing platform owners should buy blowers as bare tools rather than switch brands.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Battery-platform lock-in is a durable moat for OPE brands; first-purchase share matters.
insights.quote: Switching brands just to buy “the best” probably isn’t worth it to introduce a whole new battery and charger.

insights.claim: Ryobi's strongest selling point is its 40-volt platform's breadth, spanning mowers and chainsaws to snow blowers, tillers, augers and log splitters, rather than any single tool's performance.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Ecosystem breadth drives Ryobi (Home Depot channel) customer lock-in.
insights.quote: making the platform, rather than any single tool’s performance, its strongest selling point.

insights.claim: Ego is extending its 56-volt battery platform beyond lawn tools into lifestyle products such as portable power stations, fans, wet-dry vacuums and a minibike.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Battery platforms are expanding into adjacent consumer-energy categories, widening addressable markets.
insights.locator: Ego's was nearly the most expensive blower

insights.claim: A leaf blower is a common first outdoor-power-equipment purchase, making it a gateway into a brand's battery ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Blowers are a customer-acquisition product for OPE battery platforms.
insights.quote: If you’re new to OPE—and a leaf blower is a common first purchase—the breadth of tools that share the battery matters.

insights.claim: Traditional 18-volt power-tool makers offer blowers on one-battery platforms, but these are not powerful enough to replace gas units, so even Ryobi uses 40-volt batteries for its most capable gas alternatives.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Higher-voltage OPE platforms are a distinct segment from pro power-tool platforms.

insights.claim: There is no standardized test method for battery blower CFM and MPH claims because the ANSI/OPEI B175.2 standard applies only to internal-combustion engines, letting brands measure differently.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Marketing specs are not comparable across brands; potential area for future standards/regulation.
insights.quote: there’s no universally adopted testing method for these specifications when it comes to battery-powered blowers (ANSI/OPEI B175.2, the standard test on the books, applies only to internal combustion engines).

insights.claim: Voltage claims are partly marketing: a '20-volt max' battery delivers essentially the same power as 18 volts, and likewise for 36 vs 40 volts.
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Consumers and analysts should discount headline voltage differences across brands.
insights.quote: an advertised 20-volt max battery or tool delivers essentially the same power as an 18-volt model, and the same goes for 36- and 40-volt options.
insights.locator: Volts: In the cordless power-tool arms race

insights.claim: Test picks and prices: Ego Power+ 880 CFM ($379, two 4Ah batteries), Skil 40V 650 CFM ($199, cheapest and quietest at 78.6 dB on high), Husqvarna 350iB ($379, one battery, 3-year warranty) and Ryobi 40V 800 CFM ($349, on sale $279).
insights.speaker: Sal Vaglica
insights.so_what: Price points cluster at $200-$380, with budget brands matching premium run time.
